stops.title: The first Helvetic constitution
text: On 12 April 1798 the Helvetic constitution came into force. France had conquered the Old Confederation a few weeks before.

The new state was one central state. The cantons were now only districts for the administration, the courts and the elections. A governor (Regierungsstatthalter) led each canton for the central government.

The constitution planned 21 cantons. The French commissioner changed the plan: he made the Bernese Oberland a canton (28 March) and made Baden with the Freie Ämter a canton (11 April). Bellinzona and Lugano became cantons on 14 April.
At first the Republic had only ten cantons. The cantons of central Switzerland refused the constitution and fought against it. Aarau was the first capital.

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Das am 12. April 1798 in Kraft getretene, von Frankreich aufoktroyierte Grundgesetz war eine Adaptation der französischen Direktorialverfassung von 1795.
sources.supports: The constitution came into force on 12 April 1798

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: In den Kampfhandlungen Anfang März 1798 ging die alte Eidgenossenschaft unter.
sources.supports: France had conquered the Old Confederation a few weeks before

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Die Kantone sanken zu blossen Verwaltungseinheiten herab; sie verfügten zwar über eine Gerichtsorganisation (Kantonsgericht, Distriktsgerichte), nicht aber über eigene Legislativen.
sources.supports: One central state; the cantons are only units for administration and courts

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Mittels der Regierungsstatthalter , der Distriktsstatthalter und der Agenten kontrollierte es theoretisch das ganze Land.
sources.supports: A governor (Regierungsstatthalter) leads each canton for the central government

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Gemäss Verfassung sollte die Helvetische Republik aus 21 Kantonen bestehen
sources.supports: The constitution planned 21 cantons

sources.title: HLS: Lugano (Kanton)
sources.quote: die vom 14. April 1798 bis 19. Februar 1803 bestand
sources.supports: Bellinzona and Lugano became cantons on 14 April 1798

sources.title: HLS: Lugano (Kanton)
sources.quote: und gleichzeitig mit dem Kanton Bellinzona gebildet wurde.
sources.supports: Bellinzona and Lugano became cantons on 14 April 1798

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Am 28. März 1798 erhob der französische Regierungskommissär François-Philibert Le Carlier das Berner Oberland zu einem eigenen Kanton
sources.supports: The French commissioner made the Oberland a canton on 28 March

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: am 11. April angesichts des Widerstands in Zug auch Baden und die Freien Ämter.
sources.supports: Baden with the Freie Ämter became a canton on 11 April

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Die Landsgemeindeorte und ein Teil der befreiten Landschaften in der Inner- und der Ostschweiz empfanden die helvetische Verfassung als Bedrohung
sources.supports: Central Switzerland refused the constitution

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Nach einer missglückten militärischen Offensive (22. April - 3. Mai 1798) nahmen die Urkantone die Konstitution gezwungenermassen an.
sources.supports: Central Switzerland fought against the constitution

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Hauptstadt der Helvetischen Republik war bis September 1798 Aarau
sources.supports: Aarau was the first capital

sources.title: HLS: Aarau
sources.quote: die am 26. März 1798 zur Hauptstadt der Helvetischen Republik ernannt wurde.
sources.supports: Aarau was the first capital

sources.title: HLS: Kantone
sources.quote: Das Gebiet der Republik wurde im Frühjahr 1798 in 10, dann 22 und schliesslich 19 ähnlich grosse Kantone eingeteilt
sources.supports: At first the Republic had only ten cantons

stops.title: Eighteen cantons
text: On 4 May 1798 the French commissioner Rapinat joined several small planned cantons into three large ones. Now the Republic had 18 cantons.

Waldstätten joined Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug. This took away votes from the cantons that were against the Republic. Linth joined Glarus with the old ruled lands along the Linth and the Rhine. Säntis joined Appenzell, St. Gallen and the Rheintal.
In the same weeks France took Geneva. The new cantons started their work in June 1798. In September 1798 the capital moved from Aarau to Lucerne.

stops.title: Rätien joins
text: On 21 April 1799 the Three Leagues (Graubünden) joined the Helvetic Republic as the canton of Rätien. In July 1798 the communes of Graubünden had voted against this. The treaty was signed while French troops held the land.

In 1799 the war between France and Austria was fought on Swiss land. Austrian troops and their Russian allies held the east of the country for some months. In 1800 French troops held Graubünden again, and the union was carried out step by step.
In May 1799 the capital moved from Lucerne to Bern.

stops.title: Central Switzerland divided again
text: Federalists (people who wanted strong cantons) took power in Bern on 27–28 October 1801. In November 1801 they divided the canton of Waldstätten again into Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug.
In the Peace of Lunéville (February 1801), Austria gave the Fricktal to France.

stops.title: The second constitution
text: In April 1802 the Unitarians (people who wanted one central state) took power again. A second Helvetic constitution was put to the first popular vote in Switzerland. It counted as accepted on 2 July 1802, because people who did not vote were counted as yes votes.
Payerne and Avenches still belong to Fribourg. They go back to Léman (Vaud) only on 16 October 1802.
The Fricktal had been its own small canton since February 1802. It was not yet part of the Republic.

stops.title: Fricktal in, Valais out
text: On 29 July 1802 the government put Bern and the Oberland under one governor. On 13 August 1802 France agreed that the Fricktal could join the Republic.
On 27 August 1802 Valais became an independent republic, separate from the Helvetic Republic. France wanted it.
At the end of July 1802 French troops left the country. Uprisings against the central government began (the 'Stecklikrieg'). Parts of Säntis broke away. Then French troops came back.

stops.title: The end of the Helvetic Republic
text: Napoleon Bonaparte, the ruler of France, gave Switzerland a new order: the Act of Mediation of 19 February 1803. On 10 March 1803 the Helvetic government gave its power to the new Landammann (head of the Confederation).
The cantons were states again. There were 19: the 13 old cantons and 6 new ones (St. Gallen, Graubünden, Aargau, Thurgau, Ticino and Vaud).
Valais, Geneva, Neuchâtel and the Jura stayed outside Switzerland until 1815.

notes: Borders follow today's municipalities and districts, so they are approximate. Oberland: only Thun, Hilterfingen, Oberhofen, Sigriswil, Heiligenschwendi, Horrenbach-Buchen and Teuffenthal are taken from today's Thun district (the eastern half of the old Amt Thun, without Steffisburg). Payerne and Avenches: the 1798 districts are approximated by 11 municipalities. Hitzkirch (in canton Baden, district Sarmenstorf, 1798-1803) is approximated by Hitzkirch, Aesch (LU) and Ermensee. Upper Toggenburg (in Linth) is approximated by Nesslau, Ebnat-Kappel and Wildhaus-Alt St. Johann; it split from Linth in 1801, but the sources do not say where it went, so the map keeps it in Linth. Rheintal: only Rüthi goes to Linth (Lienz is part of Altstätten today). Biel is Biel/Bienne and Evilard; the Birseck is the Arlesheim district without Binningen, Bottmingen, Birsfelden, Münchenstein, Muttenz and Biel-Benken (which belonged to Basel). Stop 1 shows the plan of April 1798; Glarus, Appenzell, St. Gallen and central Switzerland were not yet in the Republic, and their planned borders are drawn only roughly. Tarasp and Rhäzüns were Austrian until 1803 but cannot be separated from today's municipalities Scuol and Rhäzüns. The second constitution (1802) planned to dissolve Waldstätten, Oberland, Baden, Bellinzona, Lugano, Linth and Säntis, and to join Baden to Aargau; the sources say Baden, Linth, Säntis, Bellinzona and Lugano still existed formally until 1803, so the 1802 stops keep them. The Fricktal was Austrian until the Peace of Lunéville (1801), not until 1802; from 1801 it was French. The date 1801-11 has no day: the source gives only 'November 1801'. Geneva: French troops came in mid-April 1798; the annexation treaty is dated 26 April 1798 (from general knowledge, not checked in a source).
